paper_title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: VLN requires an embodied agent to connect movement decisions with precise movement [4, 13, 27, 28, 36, 47]. Representative methods adapt general-purpose VLM through navigation-domain supervision to predict geometric goals for an action expert [20, 49] or generate numerical movement commands in predefined format [13]. However, we observe substantial displacement of the base VLMs weights and degraded performance of general visual capability following this adaptation, as shown in Figure 1. Inspired by DeepSeek-R1-Zero [21], which demonstrates that reasoning capabilities can emerge through RL directly from base language model without prior SFT, we introduce ZeroVLN, the first slowfast navigation framework that learns navigation through environment interaction with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than adapting the brain to predict geometric goals, we introduce semantic tool interface that connects it to trainable flow-matching action expert [54]. Through natural-language tool calls, the brain conveys movement decisions to the action expert, which translates them into continuous motion. Within this framework, we first construct reference trajectories from the brains own movement requests, collected through online rollouts with the brain frozen. To ground these requests in executable motion, we design privileged trajectory planner that leverages semantic map derived from the scene mesh [35]. The resulting reference trajectories are paired with their originating requests to provide semantically aligned supervision for the action expert. We then jointly optimize the brains movement decisions and the action experts continuous execution through multi-round agentic RL [18, 61]. To address sparse success signals in challenging long-horizon navigation 1 tasks, we design complementary process and outcome rewards that distinguish useful progress even when task completion fails. Beyond conventional slowfast frameworks, our design provides two key benefits: (1) the semantic interface leverages the brains native capabilities for flexible tool use and feedback-driven recovery [29, 56]; (2) Rather than specializing the model for navigation through SFT, ZeroVLN builds upon its existing language and navigation decision-making capabilities, using RL to enhance navigation performance while largely preserving its general-purpose abilities. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce ZeroVLN, the first slowfast VLN framework that connects VLM brain with an action expert policy through semantic tool interface, achieving zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. We develop two-stage training paradigm that first aligns continuous execution with the brains semantic requests through request-grounded supervision and execution-prefix learning, then jointly optimizes the slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL. Across mainstream VLN-CE benchmarks, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based baselines trained on the same navigation episodes, with only 0.01497% VLM weight displacement while largely preserving general visual capabilities. Figure 1 General Capability after Navigation Adaptation. Compared with the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B model, DualVLN loses substantial accuracy on most visual and spatial benchmarks, motivating navigation learning without brain SFT.

sections.title: 2 Architecture
sections.content: Semantic Tool Calls and Contextual Queries. As illustrated in Figure 2, we separate movement decisions from continuous motion execution through semantic tool-calling interface. Rather than predicting geometric goals, the VLM brain makes movement decisions via run_action_head(target, where, plan), specifying target, its relative location, and local plan for the action expert. The brain can also inspect the scene through turn(direction, degrees) or terminate navigation through stop(reason), with prompts and tool schemas detailed in Appendix G.1. At slow decision round t, the brain policy πθ generates tool call yt from multimodal context xt, including the navigation instruction, RGB observations, tool history, and trajectory trace. For movement calls, qt denotes the natural-language arguments of yt. To convey the request and its navigation context to the action expert, we concatenate learnable query embeddings with the embedded context and tool call. The VLM contextualizes these queries, whose final-layer hidden states Qt provide the action expert with semantic conditioning [49]: Qt = [VLMθ (Embed(xt, yt) Q)]Q . sections.title: 3 Learning to Execute Semantic Requests
sections.content: Request-Grounded Anchoring. Our semantic interface also changes how action expert supervision must be constructed. Geometric-interface VLN frameworks can derive training conditions directly from scene meshes or ground-truth trajectories [3, 20, 49], whereas our action expert follows natural-language requests issued online by the brain itself. Directly constructing semantic requests may not match the brains actual request distribution, leaving the action expert exposed to out-of-distribution instructions at inference. Generating requests online along fixed trajectories also leaves the action labels independent of the requested movement. We report results for these alternatives, including CAST-inspired augmentation [19] and request transfer in Appendix D.2. Figure 4 Request Grounding And Reference Trajectory Generation. The trajectory planner maps the original movement request to scene instance and reachable endpoint. Red curves mark grounding correspondences. Semantic maps and mesh geometry are used only during training. Built upon these insights, we propose request-grounded data construction strategy that generates trajectories from the brains actual requests. To realize this, we design privileged semantic planner that uses mesh-derived semantic map [35] and training-only geometry to ground each request qt at the agents current , from which reference trajectory ρt is planned. As shown in Table 1, ZeroVLN learns navigation from 34,445 training episodes without dataset-provided expert trajectories or navigation-domain supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the VLM brain. On SAGE-3D, it achieves 51.3% SR, surpassing NaVILA-SAGEs 46.0% with roughly 1/14 as many training episodes. On R2R and RxR, ZeroVLN surpasses Uni-NaVid by 13.4% and 9.1% in OSR, respectively, with corresponding SR gains of 5.7% and 2.7%. Together, these results demonstrate that ZeroVLN offers data-efficient alternative to navigation-specific brain adaptation while achieving competitive VLN-CE performance. ZeroVLN outperforms SFT-based VLN frameworks with the same backbone and training data. DualVLN has to learn both geometric goal prediction and action execution [49], while NaVILA [13] benefits from simpler training setup, as its predicted motion commands are executed directly by the simulator without requiring 8 learned action controller. This helps explain its consistently stronger performance than DualVLN across all benchmarks and metrics. Despite also learning continuous action control like DualVLN, ZeroVLN avoids requiring the VLM brain to learn navigation-specific output interface. Instead, request-grounded supervision teaches the action expert to execute the brains natural-language requests, while joint RL further aligns semantic decisions with continuous execution. Under the same backbone and training episodes, ZeroVLN outperforms DualVLN by over 30% in SR across all three benchmarks. Notably, it also surpasses NaVILA, whose motion commands are executed directly by the simulator without learned action controller, by 27.8%, 6.2%, and 2.7% on SAGE-3D, R2R, and RxR, respectively. The flexibility of semantic tool use comes with trade-off in path efficiency. On R2R and RxR, ZeroVLN achieves higher OSR than NaVILA (66.7% and 64.6% vs. 51.8% and 55.6%), but lower SPL (29.2% and 28.1% vs. 41.8% and 43.0%). Rather than imitating dataset-provided expert trajectories, ZeroVLN learns through interaction, allowing the agent to recover from blocked movement by revising its requests and exploring alternative paths. This flexibility improves goal reachability, although the additional exploration can lead to longer navigation paths and lower SPL. Figure 6 Navigation Training Mechanisms. SFT fits the brain to prescribed navigation outputs. ZeroVLN instead reinforces its sampled semantic requests through navigation returns, building on the brains existing capabilities. ZeroVLN learns navigation while largely preserving the VLM brains general capabilities. As illustrated in Figure 6, Navigation SFT reshapes the brains output distribution to fit navigation-specific targets, whereas our joint RL reinforces or suppresses the brains own sampled tool-call token paths according to trajectory-level advantages. This distinction in training signals is reflected in the extent of VLM parameter changes. As shown in Figure 7, ZeroVLN induces only 0.01497% relative VLM weight displacement [26, 51], compared with 3.21% for DualVLN and 7.67% for NaVILA. This substantially smaller parameter shift is accompanied by stronger retention of general visual capabilities. In spatial reasoning example, both the base and ZeroVLN-tuned brains correctly identify the tray as the nearest object, whereas DualVLN and NaVILA generate navigation commands. Such cases are not isolated. Across twelve general visual benchmarks, ZeroVLN retains 59.16% mean accuracy, close to the base brains 59.47%, while both SFT baselines score zero. These qualitative and quantitative results jointly demonstrate that ZeroVLN can acquire navigation capabilities with minimal changes to the VLM brain while largely preserving its general visual capabilities. The Base Brain Already Makes Useful Navigation Decisions. As shown in Table 1, Direct Tool Use achieves 39.5% SR on SAGE-3D without navigation training, demonstrating that general-purpose VLM can already leverage instructions and visual observations to make useful navigation decisions, which provides the foundation for our request-grounded supervision. Figure 9 Execution-Prefix versus Full-Sequence Supervision. With identical reference trajectories and frozen brain, supervising the executed prefix yields stronger navigation performance and provides useful initialization for joint RL. Execution-Prefix Action Expert Adaptation Provides Strong Initialization for RL. As shown in Figure 9, semantically aligned action adaptation raises SR from 27.0% to 37.5% on SAGE-3D and from 11.6% to 17.4% on average across R2R and RxR. The supervision strategy also matters: on identical reference trajectories, execution-prefix supervision consistently outperforms full-sequence supervision, validating its better alignment with actual execution. The adapted policy achieves mean Pass@4 of 43.5% on R2R/RxR, improving the likelihood of sampling successful rollouts. This provides stronger exploration policy for group-relative RL, mitigating degenerate advantage estimates under sparse terminal rewards. Figure 10 Recovery from Blocked Motion in R2R. The brain changes its view and revises blocked climbing requests, reaches the second landing, and stops at round 25, illustrating feedback-driven coordination with the action expert. Joint RL Translates Local Execution into End-to-End Navigation Success. While supervised adaptation teaches 11 the action expert to follow individual movement requests, successful navigation requires coordinating successive semantic decisions and continuous executions. As shown in Table 1, joint RL raises SR from 17.0% to 52.7% on R2R, from 18.7% to 51.4% on RxR, and from 36.9% to 51.3% on SAGE-3D. The staircase example in Figure 10 illustrates this multi-round coordination. After encountering blocked motion, the brain changes its view and revises its movement request, which the action expert executes to reach the second landing before the brain successfully stops. This demonstrates how coordinated semantic decisions and continuous execution support recovery from local failures and successful completion of long-horizon navigation tasks.

sections.title: 5.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: Figure 11 Round-Level versus Trajectory-Level RLOO. Under matched rewards, trajectory-level credit improves SR and SPL, lowers NE, and narrows the OSRSR gap, better connecting goal reaching with successful completion. Trajectory-level advantages favor task completion and path efficiency, whereas round-level advantages emphasize goal reaching. We compare the two credit assignment strategies under identical reward settings. As shown in Figure 11, round-level advantages achieve higher OSR but exhibit declining SR and increasing NE during training, whereas trajectory-level advantages yield higher SR and SPL with lower NE, indicating more reliable task completion and better path efficiency despite fewer goal visits. The key difference lies in how credit is assigned. Round-level advantages can reinforce goal-reaching decision even if subsequent actions lead to failure, whereas trajectory-level advantages assign all rounds the same advantage derived from the complete navigation return. By accounting for both goal arrival and terminal success, trajectory-level credit favors decisions that contribute to successful task completion rather than isolated goal visits. Implementation details of the round-level variant are provided in Appendix B.7. Figure 12 Joint Optimization and Reward Ablations. Joint RL sustains improvements beyond updating either policy alone. Removing arrival, terminal-success, or process rewards weakens goal reaching, task completion, or training stability. Joint optimization enables coordinated adaptation of movement decisions and action execution. As shown in 12 Figure 12 (top), updating only the action expert yields limited improvements, suggesting that better execution alone cannot overcome the limitations of fixed semantic decisions. In contrast, updating only the brain initially improves navigation, but SR and OSR subsequently decline below initialization. This behavior is consistent with growing mismatch between the brains evolving movement requests and the fixed action expert. Joint RL, however, achieves sustained improvements across navigation metrics by allowing both policies to adapt improving either together. These results highlight the importance of coordinated slowfast optimization: policy in isolation is insufficient when successful navigation depends on their continued alignment. Figure 13 (top) confirms this pattern under round-level credit: Joint RL improves SR and SPL beyond updating either policy alone. Figure 13 Joint Optimization and Rewards under Round-Level Credit. We obtain conclusions consistent with those under trajectory-level credit (Figure 12). Each component of our reward design plays significant role in sustaining stable navigation learning. We ablate each reward component under fixed trajectory-level credit assignment, as shown in Figure 12 (bottom). (1) Ablation of Outcome Rewards. Removing the first-arrival reward severely degrades navigation performance across metrics, particularly OSR, demonstrating that the sparsity of terminal success rewards makes it difficult to learn effective goal-reaching behavior without denser intermediate feedback. The first-arrival reward bridges this gap by providing more immediate signal upon reaching the goal. Conversely, without terminal success, OSR remains high while other metrics deteriorate, suggesting that rewarding arrival alone encourages goal visits rather than successful termination. These results demonstrate that the two outcome rewards must work together to balance goal reaching and task completion. (2) Ablation of Process Rewards. The process rewards further support learning when outcome rewards are scarce. Distance progress guides movement toward the goal, while information discovery encourages useful observation even without immediate spatial progress. Removing either weakens or destabilizes training, demonstrating their complementary roles in sustaining navigation improvement. We observe consistent trends under round-level credit assignment in Figure 13, further supporting the complementary roles of goal-reaching and completion rewards.

sections.title: 5.4 Consistency between Predicted Trajectories and Planner Goals
sections.content: We assess the consistency between predicted trajectories and planner-grounded local goals before and after joint RL. Under identical observations and noise seeds, we measure the endpoint distances and angular deviations of predicted action sequences relative to the local goals. As shown in Figure 14, both stages exhibit low endpoint distances and angular deviations, demonstrating that supervised adaptation establishes goal-following behavior that is largely preserved after joint RL. 13 Figure 14 Consistency between predicted trajectories and planner goals before and after joint RL, with additional details provided in Appendix E.2.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce ZeroVLN, the first slowfast VLN framework that enables general-purpose VLM brain to guide action expert execution through semantic tool use, without navigation-domain SFT. We combine requestgrounded and execution-prefix supervision with joint agentic RL, achieving strong navigation performance with limited data while largely preserving the VLMs general capabilities. Beyond navigation, this paradigm opens path toward general-purpose embodied agents that acquire diverse physical skills through specialized action experts while retaining shared VLM brain.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: SlowFast Systems for Navigation. Slowfast architectures separate semantic planning from motion execution, allowing each policy to operate at its own timescale. Mobility VLA [16] uses long-context VLM to select goal frame from demonstration tour and topological navigation policy to reach it. NavGPT2 [62] connects frozen language models vision-language representations to navigation policy network. DualVLN [49] trains its planner to predict pixel goals before learning contextual queries and flow-matching action expert. ABot-N1 [20] similarly uses supervised reasoning and affordance pixels to guide fast waypoint predictor. Beyond navigation, SmolVLA [44] decouples action prediction and execution through asynchronous inference, while Fast-in-Slow [8] partially shares parameters between slow reasoning and fast manipulation and coordinates them through dual-aware co-training. ZeroVLN retains this separation of planning and execution but connects the two policies through semantic requests, avoiding navigation-domain SFT for geometric goal prediction. Navigation Planning with Existing Executors. Navigation agents can use language-model reasoning to select actions executed by an external system. NavGPT [63] reasons over textual observations, navigation history, and candidate directions, while MapGPT [9] adds linguistic map and adaptive multi-step planning. SayNav [39] grounds language-model plans in an incrementally constructed 3D scene graph and delegates their execution to an existing low-level navigation policy. AgenticNav [29] exposes movement, depth, and memory as callable tools, with the harness converting selected image pixels into executable motion. NaVILA [13] instead predicts numerical movement commands in language. In the VLN-CE simulation setting considered here, these commands are executed by the system. Its legged-robot setting additionally uses learned visual locomotion policy. ETP-R1 [53] applies closed-loop GRPO to topological planning while retaining the underlying controller. Beyond selecting calls to an existing executor, ZeroVLN learns the executor itself by treating the continuous-action head as trainable tool. Privileged Supervision for Navigation Action Policies. Privileged geometry can supervise motion without requiring human demonstration for every observation. For high-speed flight, Loquercio et al. [32] train sensorimotor policy in simulation by imitating privileged expert, mapping onboard observations directly to collision-free trajectories. iPlanner [52] backpropagates trajectory costs through differentiable geometric costmap, while ViPlanner [41] incorporates semantic costs to distinguish traversable surfaces and obstacles. NavDP [6] uses privileged simulation information to learn both trajectory generation and critic-based trajectory evaluation from local RGB-D observations. CAST [19] addresses instruction following by constructing counterfactual instructionaction labels from existing robot data. In contrast, ZeroVLN starts from the brains actual movement requests and uses privileged trajectory planner to generate matching reference trajectories. Agentic RL and Credit Assignment. DeepSeek-R1 [21], DAPO [55], and GSPO [60] improve language-model reasoning through RL. SAGE [23] targets reasoning efficiency, while R2M [24] aligns reward feedback with the evolving policy. Extending RL to multi-round agents requires connecting delayed outcomes to the decisions that produced them. ReTool [17] interleaves language reasoning with code execution and uses outcome rewards to learn when and how to invoke tools. GiGPO [18] combines episode-level advantages with step-level comparisons at repeated environment states. PGPO [61] estimates state potentials from grouped rollout returns to distinguish intermediate actions. Agent Lightning [33] decomposes agent trajectories into training transitions, while Agent-R1 [14] separates generated outputs from environment feedback during policy optimization. VAGEN [46] introduces explicit world-model reasoning and bi-level credit assignment for visually grounded agents. In autonomous driving, DEFT-RLVR [25] combines verifiable trajectory selection with rubric-based reasoning rewards, assigning shared credit across its two-stage interaction. ZeroVLN adapts trajectory-level credit to navigation through complementary process and outcome rewards that account for exploration, goal reaching, and task completion. Reinforcement Learning for Generative Action Policies. Generative action policies require optimization through their action-generation process. Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization [40] applies policy gradients to diffusion denoising steps for continuous control. Flow-GRPO [31] converts deterministic flow sampling into stochastic paths to enable online group-relative optimization, providing mechanism applicable to flow-based action generation. Flow Policy Gradients [54] instead optimizes expressive flow policies without explicit likelihood computation for robot control. ConRFT [12] combines behavior cloning and Q-learning for offline VLA adaptation, followed by online consistency-policy optimization with human interventions. RIPT-VLA [45] uses interactive rollouts and leave-one-out advantages to adapt VLA policies from sparse success rewards. Building on action-policy RL, ZeroVLN is, to our knowledge, the first to jointly optimize VLM brain and continuous-action expert through agentic RL in VLN-CE. History Modeling and Spatial Planning. Navigation policies use history to maintain spatial context beyond the current observation. HAMT [10] jointly encodes the instruction, past panoramic observations, and current view. DUET [11] combines local visual grounding with global topological map for long-range planning. BEVBert [2] learns multimodal map representations that combine local metric structure with global topology, supporting spatial reasoning and long-range planning. GridMM [48] organizes historical observations in an egocentric grid memory and aggregates instruction-relevant visual features. ETPNav [3] constructs an online topological map from predicted waypoints and couples cross-modal planning with an obstacle-avoiding controller. ZeroVLN likewise retains historical context, but supplies interaction records and the executed trajectory trace directly to the brain for semantic tool decisions.

sections.title: B Additional Details of Model Architecture and Training Paradigm
sections.content: B.1 Action Expert Architecture Figure 3 illustrates our action expert. We provide all numerical settings and parameter counts in Appendix D.1, including Tables 2 and 3. The architecture follows the dual-stream conditioning design of DualVLN [49]. Our implementation uses query-based visual pooler and condition-fusion Transformer to combine the movement request with reference and current views. Fusing Reference and Current Views. Execution verification rejects position errors reaching 0.035 or heading errors reaching 2. Open-Loop Adaptation and Joint RL Settings. Both training stages use AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, numerical epsilon 108, and no learning-rate warmup. Weight decay is 0.01 during open-loop adaptation and zero during RL. Open-loop training runs on four 16-device nodes, with one slow anchor per device per training step, global batch of 64 anchors, and gradient clipping at 1. Each anchor contains four execution cycles. We sample SAGE-3D, R2R, and RxR at ratio of 1:1:2 in open-loop training and optimize the queries and action expert at constant learning rate of 5 105. For flow-matching supervision, the logit-normal flow-time distribution uses an underlying normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Each epoch contains 6,014 training steps. The RL initialization follows 10,826 training steps, or approximately 1.8 epochs. RL uses eight 16-device nodes and samples the datasets at ratio of 2:1:1. Each training step contains 64 episodes with eight rollouts each, totaling 512 rollouts. The brain, queries, and action expert use constant learning rate of 106, while the fast visual backbone remains frozen. The RL training budget is 200 training steps. We set the return discount γ = 1 for both credit estimators, the text-loss weight λtext = 0.1, and the action-advantage clipping threshold amax = 1. Distance progress, first arrival, and terminal success each have weight 1. We set Ninfo = 5 and winfo = 0.01, capping the information reward at 0.05 per episode. Distance progress uses dmin = 1 m. The action sampler uses three uniform Flow-SDE transitions from = 1 through = 2/3 and = 1/3 to = 0, with noise scale 0.08. The drift step is 1/3, and the Gaussian variance uses its absolute value. The numerical variance floor is 106. The main single-training-step action objective is evaluated at the rollout policy, as in Eq. (18). Context Management. The brain has 131,072-token context limit, with thinking disabled throughout collection, RL, and navigation evaluation. Supervision collection uses temperature 1.0 and top-p 0.95, with 256-token text budget. RL sampling uses temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0, no top-k truncation or repetition, 29 presence, or frequency penalties, and 512-token completion limit per round. Navigation evaluation uses temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95, with 256-token text budget excluding reserved query tokens. Action expert data collection and RL allow 100 and 50 rounds per episode, respectively. On SAGE-3D, the navigation camera provides 640480 RGB observations with horizontal field of view of 115 at height of 1.2 m. We append tool calls, execution feedback, and observations to the interaction history. Only the final image of movement call is appended as the next slow observation, separately from the tool result that reports motion and execution status. Intermediate images condition fast execution. During long evaluation episodes, history is compressed only when the input, output budget, and an 8,192-token reserve exceed the service window. Compression retains the initial task and recent eight rounds, samples one complete round from every four older rounds, and removes older past-trajectory snapshots while preserving the latest cumulative trajectory. In Figure 12, SR and NE are averaged equally over R2R and RxR, while SPL is averaged equally over SAGE-3D, R2R, and RxR. Its OSR is the equal-weight mean of SAGE-3D arrival success and R2R/RxR OSR. The direct credit-assignment comparison in Section 5.3 holds rewards and update settings fixed and compares round-level and trajectorylevel advantage estimation. In Figure 11, all four metrics (SR, OSR, SPL, and NE) are averaged equally over R2R and RxR, and the OSRSR gap is computed from these same averages. Together, these three ablations test how credit coordinates decisions across rounds, whether both policies need to adapt, and which reward signals sustain navigation learning. D.2 Why Supervision Should Follow the Brains Requests We examine why the action expert should learn from the brains actual requests, as proposed in Section 3. The alternatives expose two distinct mismatches: constructed requests can differ from the brains language, and fixed demonstration trajectories can differ from its intended movement. Constructed Requests Do Not Guarantee Navigation Transfer. We design request augmentation to make the action expert distinguish movement intentions under identical visual observations, rather than predict motion from the scene alone. Inspired by CAST [19], we construct paired movement requests at the same navigation state while keeping the brain frozen  (Table 5)  . Direction augmentation pairs leftward and rightward diagonal trajectories with corresponding language templates in the tool calls plan field. Object/relation augmentation changes the requested object or the side from which it is approached, pairing each request with its corresponding geometrically verified trajectory. We retain the original data and add these requesttrajectory pairs to train the contextual queries and action expert. On 67 held-out state pairs evaluated with four shared noise seeds, the action expert learns these requests well: paired direction accuracy rises from 0% to 95.90% on the training template and reaches 96.27% on held-out template  (Table 6)  . Yet high template accuracy does not translate into better closed-loop navigation. On the same 100 SAGE-3D episodes with four rollouts per episode and 50-call budget, final navigation SR is 13.25%, equal to training without augmentation, despite 30 direction accuracy remaining above 92% in Figure 15a,b. These augmentation runs use one training seed and different training exposure. Table 5 Data for Scene-Conditioned Augmentation. Pairs are counterfactual pairs; samples are execution cycles. Direction augmentation uses two directions and three templates per pair. Object/relation augmentation retains two branches and up to four cycles per pair. Training Data Original Data Direction Augmentation Object/Relation Augmentation Pairs 49,647 19,114 Anchors 124,458 297,882 Samples 465,973 297, 38,228 134,930 Request Distribution Matters beyond Geometric Validity. Among 456 brain-generated requests evaluated with the same four noise seeds, 199 groups contain both left and right movement requests under the same state and request family. Paired heading accuracy on these 199 pairs is 64.70% without augmentation and 56.91% with augmentation  (Table 6)  . These requests also differ from the templates: none of the 456 sampled plans uses the explicit diagonal-motion terms employed in direction augmentation. Thus, an action expert can learn the constructed languagemotion associations without reliably transferring them to the language used during navigation. The missing alignment concerns how the brain expresses its intention, not merely whether the supervised trajectory is feasible. This motivates collecting requests from the frozen brain itself, so action expert adaptation targets the language it will encounter during interaction. For the paired tests in Table 6, constructed requests require correct lateral directions, at least 5 cm displacement, and collision-free static replay; brain-generated requests require correct heading directions in both In Figure 15a,b, direction and object/relation tests use 67 and 25 pairs, respectively, prediction prefixes. with four samples per pair. Object/relation tests require collision-free motion, trajectory error below 0.5 m, and closer agreement with the requested branch. The dashed line denotes training without augmentation. Curves connect evaluated policies without smoothing. Natural Requests Need Corresponding Motion Targets. GT-Route Anchoring aims to combine the brains natural request distribution with readily available expert trajectories, avoiding the need to plan new trajectory for every request. We first place slow anchors along dataset-provided expert trajectories. At each anchor, the frozen brain receives the navigation instruction, current and historical RGB observations, previous tool interactions, and the past trajectory trace, then generates movement call with target, where, and plan arguments. The brain does not see the future expert trajectory. We sample eight calls per anchor and retain up to four valid, deduplicated history branches without filtering calls by their directional agreement with the trajectory. Each retained call is paired with the original trajectorys subsequent action labels, and the next anchors observations and execution feedback are obtained by replaying that trajectory. Thus, the expert trajectory determines the visited states and motion targets, while the brain generates the requests from those states. Different requests can consequently receive the same motion target. Request-Grounded Anchoring instead plans reference trajectory for each generated request. Figure 15c,d compares the complete pipelines on 100 episodes each: GT-Route Anchoring uses one rollout per episode with 200 calls, while Request-Grounded Anchoring uses four rollouts with 100 calls. The best-SR GT-Route policy reaches 34.0% SR and 21.55% Table 6 Transfer from Constructed to Brain-Generated Requests. SPL, while our RL initialization reaches 37.5% and 22.56%, with differences in episode subsets, contexts, executors, and training exposure between the pipelines. Together, these comparisons motivate an open-loop training scheme that aligns both the source of requests and their motion targets. Constructed requests can teach local control without transferring to the brains language, while attaching natural requests to fixed expert trajectories does not ensure that the labels execute those requests. Our key design choice is to let the frozen brains requests determine the supervision: the planner constructs corresponding reference trajectory, allowing the action expert to learn the movements the brain actually asks it to perform. Execution-prefix supervision further aligns this learning with visual replanning, supported by the matched-trajectory comparison in Figure 9. This request-to-trajectory construction enables semantic action expert adaptation without navigation SFT of the brain or dataset-provided expert trajectories. D.3 Direct Tool Use Baseline We evaluate the original Qwen3.6-35B-A3B checkpoint using four simulator-executed tools: move_forward(distance), move_backward(distance), turn(direction, degrees), and stop(reason). The VLM receives no navigation SFT or RL. Forward and backward requests specify distance between 0.05 and 5 m, and turning requests specify left or right rotation between 0.5 and 90. The harness executes translations in substeps of at most 0.25 and returns the actual movement, blocked status, and updated RGB observation. Each response permits one tool call. Invalid or multiple calls receive error feedback and consume one decision before the model retries. The model observes the task instruction, up to eight recent RGB images including the current view, textual tool history, and the latest diagram of its executed trajectory. The diagram is built from actual relative movement and heading, with markers for blocked motion and collisions. Goal coordinates, reference routes, and evaluator success signals are withheld from the policy. Sampling uses temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95, with thinking disabled and maximum of 256 output tokens per decision. We run one rollout per episode on all 944 SAGE-3D, 1,839 R2R, and 3,669 English RxR episodes. Each episode allows up to 200 interaction rounds. Appendix G.2 presents the baseline instructions in English along with its tool schemas. D.4 Controlled Comparisons with SFT-Based VLN Baselines We use the official open-source implementations of NaVILA [13] and DualVLN [49], replacing only their VLM backbones and training episodes with the same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone and 34,445 source episodes used by ZeroVLN, while preserving their original data augmentation, supervision construction, training procedures, action representations, and motion scales. NaVILA expands the source demonstrations into 1,305,082 motioncommand samples and fine-tunes the full VLM backbone for one epoch with global batch size of 64. DualVLN retains its two-stage procedure of first learning pixel-goal prediction, then freezing the brain and 32 training continuous-action expert. The two stages use 1,539,344 and 1,126,788 distinct supervision samples and complete 12,027 and 8,804 training steps, respectively, with global batch size of 128. Continuation uses previously unused samples and covers the full eligible fast-policy sample pool. NaVILAs supervision sample count is 3.39 times our semantic anchor count, while DualVLNs two stages use 4.00 and 2.93 times as many samples, respectively. Our comparison thus uses the same backbone and source data while preserving both baselines native pipelines for expanding supervision, without restricting their sample counts to the number of semantic anchors used by ZeroVLN. D.5 Measuring General Capabilities and Weight Displacement We evaluate the shared Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone, ZeroVLN, DualVLN, and NaVILA on twelve general visual and spatial benchmarks. Table 7 provides the complete results. Weight displacement measures the extent of parameter change, while benchmark performance evaluates the preservation of general response capabilities, providing complementary evidence at the parameter and functional levels. Shared Inputs and Scoring Criteria. All four models receive the same evaluation examples, images, questions, answer options, and benchmark-specific prompts through VLMEvalKit, without navigation system prompts or tool schemas. We use temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, maximum output length of 32,768 tokens, and seed 3407, with thinking disabled. The presence and repetition penalties are 1.5 and 1.0, respectively, and min-p is 0. Each benchmark uses the same answer parser and scoring rules across models. Multiple-choice answers are extracted and scored with the rule-based exact_matching evaluator rather than an LLM judge. Spatial localization answers follow the corresponding benchmarks native scoring rules. For example, the EmbSpatialBench prompt requests the selected option letter in JSON answer field. We report the vanilla score for 3DSRBench and average the twelve benchmark scores with equal weights. Relative Weight Displacement. We represent navigation adaptation as task vector, following Ilharco et al. [26]. Let θpre contain the inherited VLM weights before navigation adaptation and θft the corresponding weights after adaptation, including RL for ZeroVLN. Li et al. [51] use the base weights as the reference for an L2 penalty in transfer learning. Building on these definitions, we normalize the weight difference by the base models norm and report the relative displacement as percentage: θ = θft θpre, drel = 100 θ2 θpre2 %. (28) We match saved checkpoint tensors by parameter name and shape and accumulate squared weight differences and squared base-weight values in double precision. The square root of their ratio gives the relative L2 displacement. We include all inherited VLM weights, including frozen weights, and count shared parameters once. New contextual queries and action heads are excluded because they have no counterpart in the base VLM. All three methods use the same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B initialization as the reference.
